title: Commercial Insurance, HMO, PPO, and Managed Care

sections.learningObjectives:
- Describe commercial insurance and its key cost-sharing terms.
- Distinguish HMO and PPO plans, including network, referral, and cost differences.
- Explain managed care concepts such as networks, referrals, prior authorization, and capitation.
- Apply the medical office assistant's role in verifying eligibility and supporting referrals and authorizations within scope.
sections.eli10:
### Question 1

Think of commercial insurance like buying a cell phone plan from a private company. The company sells you a plan you pay for, and it helps cover your costs when you need care.

### Question 2

The payer is like the bank that pays the restaurant bill on your behalf after you have paid your membership fee.

### Question 3

The premium is like your monthly subscription fee to a streaming service. You pay it every month just to keep the service available.

### Question 4

The deductible is like the first part of a long road trip you pay for out of your own gas money before the insurance helps pay for the rest.

### Question 5

A copay is like a small admission ticket you pay each time you go to the movies; the insurance company pays the rest of the movie.

### Question 6

Coinsurance is like splitting a pizza by percent: the plan pays for 8 slices and you pay for 2 slices of the cost.

### Question 7

The out-of-pocket maximum is like a safety cap on a water bill; once you pay up to the cap, the plan picks up everything else for the year.

### Question 8

Commercial insurance is like a store-bought plan from a private company, while government programs are like plans run by the government for certain groups of people.

### Question 9

Group coverage is like a school buying a big bundle of supplies for the whole class so each student pays less than buying alone.

### Question 10

The subscriber is like the team captain whose name is on the roster; everyone else on the plan is listed under that captain.

### Question 11

A dependent is like a family member added to the family phone plan under the account holder's name.

### Question 12

Verifying eligibility is like checking that a gift card still has money on it before the customer tries to pay.

### Question 13

The member ID is like your student ID number; it tells the school exactly which student you are.

### Question 14

COB is like deciding which of two parents pays for dinner first so the restaurant is not paid twice.

### Question 15

The primary payer is like the first friend to chip in for a group gift; the second friend covers what is left.

### Question 16

A benefits summary is like the menu at a restaurant that tells you what is included and what costs extra.

### Question 17

Collecting the copay is like taking the entry ticket at the door so the account is settled before the movie starts.

### Question 18

Answering coverage questions is like checking a library book's availability; you look it up rather than guessing from memory.

### Question 19

An HMO is like a club where you pick one main doctor who helps guide all your care within the club's team.

### Question 20

An HMO is like a gym membership where you can only use that gym's own equipment, not any gym in town.

### Question 21

The gatekeeper PCP is like a hallway monitor who must give you a pass before you can visit a specialist's room.

### Question 22

A referral is like a permission slip from your main teacher before you can visit the music room.

### Question 23

An HMO is like having a coach who helps you stay healthy and plans your whole team's training schedule.

### Question 24

An HMO is like a less expensive club membership that comes with fewer choices of where to go.

### Question 25

Going out of network in an HMO is like shopping at a store your membership card does not work at; you pay full price.

### Question 26

Emergency care is like calling the fire department; you use the nearest help right away, and the plan handles the rules afterward.

### Question 27

A PPO is like a membership that gives you a discount at its favorite stores but still lets you shop elsewhere for a higher price.

### Question 28

A PPO is like a flexible bus pass that works on many routes, even if some routes cost a little more.

### Question 29

A PPO specialist visit is like being able to visit a tutor directly without asking your homeroom teacher for a pass.

### Question 30

Out-of-network in a PPO is like buying at a store outside your discount club; you can still shop, but the discount is smaller.

### Question 31

A PPO is like paying more for an all-access pass instead of a one-park-only ticket.

### Question 32

A PPO is like being able to call any expert directly instead of going through a switchboard operator first.

### Question 33

Choosing a PPO is like picking an all-inclusive travel pass that works in many cities over a pass good in only one town.

### Question 34

An HMO is like a discount store membership: less expensive if you are happy shopping only there.

### Question 35

An in-network provider is like a store that has agreed to give club members a special discount.

### Question 36

Out-of-network is like a store that does not accept your membership card, so you might pay the regular, higher price.

### Question 37

A referral is a note from your main doctor to see a specialist, while prior authorization is the insurance company saying yes to paying for a treatment.

### Question 38

Prior authorization is like asking a parent for permission before going on a field trip, so you know it is approved ahead of time.

### Question 39

Getting prior authorization is like getting a green light before crossing; you check with the plan before moving ahead.

### Question 40

Capitation is like paying a flat monthly fee for unlimited rides instead of paying per ride.

### Question 41

Fee-for-service is like paying a taxi for each ride, while managed care is like a bus pass with set routes.

### Question 42

A formulary is like a restaurant's menu of approved dishes the plan will help pay for.

### Question 43

Utilization review is like a coach checking that each practice drill is really needed before the team runs it.

### Question 44

The PCP is like your main coach who knows your whole training plan and points you to the right specialist when needed.

### Question 45

A specialist is like a master chef who cooks only desserts instead of all dishes.

### Question 46

An EPO is like a club pass that lets you move freely among the club's own rooms but does not work at other clubs.

### Question 47

A POS plan is like a menu where you can choose a cheaper in-network option or pay more to go elsewhere.

### Question 48

In-network care is like using a coupon at a store that already agreed to give members a lower price.

### Question 49

Balance billing is like a store charging you the difference between the sale price and the full price after your coupon.

### Question 50

The network is like a team roster of doctors and hospitals your plan has already made a deal with.

### Question 51

Checking insurance is like the front-desk worker confirming your library card before you check out books.

### Question 52

Tracking referrals is like making sure the permission slip is signed before the class leaves for the trip.

### Question 53

Checking insurance each visit is like checking your lunch card balance every day before buying lunch.

### Question 54

Picking a plan is like choosing which bicycle to buy; the assistant can show the options but should not pick for the customer.

### Question 55

Updating a card is like carefully saving a new address in your contact list so messages go to the right place.

### Question 56

Flagging inactive coverage is like telling the driver the gas gauge reads empty instead of pretending it is full.

### Question 57

Collecting the copay is like charging only the ticket price at the door and letting the rest be handled later.

### Question 58

Checking the directory is like looking at the official store list instead of guessing which stores take your card.

### Question 59

Handling a denial is like reading the referee's ruling and filing the right appeal instead of replaying the same move.

### Question 60

A denial is like a no answer from a judge; you gather more evidence and ask again the proper way instead of breaking the rules.

### Question 61

The benefit year is like a fresh report card every 12 months; your totals reset when the new year starts.

### Question 62

If a pizza costs $100 and you pay 20 cents of every dollar, you pay $20 and the plan pays $80.

### Question 63

The deductible is like a savings jar you must fill with your own money first; this $150 goes into the jar.

### Question 64

Preventive care is like free routine maintenance on a car to catch problems before they grow.

### Question 65

A grandfathered plan is like an old rule book that is allowed to keep some of its original rules even after the game updates.

### Question 66

Employer coverage is like a shared lunch tab where the company and the worker each pay part.

### Question 67

This is like reminding a member their card only works at certain stores and showing them which nearby stores are on the list.

### Question 68

If someone says the house smells like smoke, you call for help right away instead of finishing the dishes.

### Question 69

A member is like a person who has a library card that lets them borrow books from the plan's library.

### Question 70

Checking plan rules is like reading the recipe before cooking instead of guessing how much salt to add.

### Question 71

Managed care is like a well-organized sports league with set teams, schedules, and rules to keep the games fair and affordable.

### Question 72

These tools are like a team's playbook of rules that keep everyone coordinated and the budget in check.

### Question 73

An HMO is like a great deal on a gym membership if you are happy using that one gym and its trainers.

### Question 74

A PPO is like a card that works at many stores, including some outside your main shopping center, for a higher price.

### Question 75

Medical necessity is like asking whether a repair is really needed to fix the car, not just a nice-to-have extra.

### Question 76

Supporting an authorization is like handing the judge only the real, relevant evidence for your case.

### Question 77

Protecting patient info is like keeping a friend's secret safe and only telling people who truly need to know to help.

### Question 78

The HMO flow is like getting a hall pass from your homeroom teacher before visiting the science lab.

### Question 79

An expired referral is like an expired hall pass; you get a new one signed instead of sneaking past.

### Question 80

Helping with cost questions is like getting a price check at the register instead of guessing what an item costs.

### Question 81

The premium is like a monthly club fee you pay even on months you never visit the club.

### Question 82

Starting early is like mailing an invitation weeks before the party instead of the day before.

### Question 83

A tiered network is like seats at a concert; the closer, more expensive seats cost you more out of pocket.

### Question 84

Open enrollment is like the sign-up week for a school club; you can join or switch only during that time.

### Question 85

Updating a plan change is like updating your delivery address so packages go to your new home.

### Question 86

Billing for services never provided is like charging a customer for food they never ordered.

### Question 87

A self-funded plan is like a company paying repair costs for its own fleet instead of buying an insurance policy for each car.

### Question 88

Verifying a caller is like asking for ID before handing over a package at the door.

### Question 89

A non-covered service is like a menu item not included in the meal deal; you tell the customer the price so they can decide.

### Question 90

HMO versus PPO is like choosing a budget pass for one gym versus a pricier pass that works at many gyms.
